name: Brisk walk
why: Walking is one of the best things for back pain: it moves the spine gently, keeps you active and builds tolerance. Short, regular walks beat one long one. Also an easy way to warm up or cool down.
setup: Wear comfortable shoes and start on flat ground.
cues: A pace where you can still talk
mistakes: Going so far that pain builds
Skipping it on sore days (go shorter instead)
feel: Comfortable effort. A little stiffness that eases as you go is fine.
stopIf: Pain spreads down your leg or keeps building as you walk.

name: Cat-cow
why: Moves your whole spine gently through rounding and arching. It eases stiffness and is a kind first exercise when the back is sore or after a run.
setup: Get on hands and knees, hands under shoulders and knees under hips.
cues: Then lift your chest and tailbone
mistakes: Forcing the end of the range
feel: Gentle movement and stretch along the back.
stopIf: Pain shoots into your leg, or one direction clearly makes the pain worse. Then stay in the comfortable range.

media.credit: Video: The Cat/Cow | Back Pain Relief Exercise (Dr. Carl Baird)

name: Pelvic tilt
why: Tiny, gentle movements of the lower back that are usually comfortable even when the back is sore. Good for easing stiffness in the morning.
setup: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat.
mistakes: Making the movement big and forceful
feel: Gentle movement in the lower back.

media.credit: Video: How to do a pelvic tilt lying down (Rehab My Patient)

name: Knee rocks
why: Gently rotates the lower back and hips. Relaxing at the end of the day, and easy on a sore back.
setup: Lie on your back with knees bent and together, feet flat.
cues: Let your knees fall slowly to one side
Bring them back, then the other way
feel: Gentle rotation and stretch in the lower back and hips.

media.credit: Video: All Care Physio - Back Exercises - Lumbar Rocks (allcarephysio)

name: Knee to chest
why: Gently rounds the lower back. Helpful when bending forward eases your back pain.
setup: Lie on your back with knees bent.
cues: Hug one knee towards your chest
feel: A stretch in the lower back and buttock.
stopIf: Pain shoots down your leg, or back pain increases.

media.credit: Video: Single Knee to Chest - Ask Doctor Jo (AskDoctorJo)

name: Child's pose
why: A gentle rounding stretch for the lower back and hips that many people find soothing, especially if bending forward eases their pain.
setup: Kneel with knees apart and big toes together.
Sit back towards your heels and walk your hands forward.
feel: A gentle stretch in the lower back and hips.
stopIf: Knee pain, or back or leg pain increases (some backs prefer arching instead).

media.credit: Video: Child's Pose Stretch (Dr. Brian Abelson)

name: Press-up (lying face down)
why: Gently arches the lower back. If standing up straight or leaning back eases your pain, repeated arching can calm it, and pain moving out of the leg towards the back is a good sign.
setup: Lie face down with your hands under your shoulders.
cues: Let your hips and back relax
mistakes: Lifting the hips off the floor
feel: Gentle pressure in the lower back that eases with repeats.
stopIf: Pain spreads further down your leg, or increases with each repeat.

name: Curl-up (McGill)
why: Trains the stomach muscles to stiffen and protect the spine without the repeated bending of a sit-up. One of McGill's 'big 3' back exercises.
setup: Lie on your back with one knee bent and the other leg straight.
Slide your hands, palms down, under the natural arch of your lower back. Swap legs halfway through.
cues: Lift head and shoulders a little, as one
mistakes: Flattening the lower back into the floor
Curling up high like a sit-up
references: McGill SM. Low Back Disorders: Evidence-Based Prevention and Rehabilitation. Human Kinetics.

media.credit: Video: McGill Big 3- Curl Up, Side Bridge, Bird Dog (freetofeelhealthy)

name: Bird dog
why: Trains the trunk muscles to keep your spine steady while your arms and legs move: the kind of endurance that protects the back when running and lifting. One of McGill's 'big 3' back exercises.
setup: Get on hands and knees, hands under shoulders, knees under hips, back flat.
cues: Reach opposite arm and leg out long
Keep your back still as a tabletop
mistakes: Lifting the leg too high and arching the back
Letting the hips tip to one side
feel: Effort in the back of the hip, along the back and around the trunk.
stopIf: Sharp back pain, or pain spreading down your leg.
references: McGill SM. Low Back Disorders: Evidence-Based Prevention and Rehabilitation. Human Kinetics.

media.credit: Video: NUH Physiotherapy - Bird Dog (National University Hospital (NUH) Singapore)

name: Side plank on knees
why: Strengthens the muscles along the side of the trunk that keep your pelvis and spine level, especially on one leg as in every running stride. The easier version of the side plank, one of McGill's 'big 3'.
setup: Lie on your side with knees bent behind you, propped on your forearm, elbow under your shoulder.
cues: Lift your hips off the floor
Straight line from head to knees
mistakes: Letting the hips sag or drift backwards
feel: Work along the side of your trunk and hip.
stopIf: Shoulder pain, or back pain increases.
references: McGill SM. Low Back Disorders: Evidence-Based Prevention and Rehabilitation. Human Kinetics.

media.credit: Video: Side Plank Too Hard? Start With This Modified Version (Physical Therapy First)

name: Side plank
why: Full side plank: strong trunk and hip support for running, hiking and lifting. One of McGill's 'big 3'.
setup: Lie on your side, legs straight and feet stacked (or top foot in front), propped on your forearm with the elbow under your shoulder.
cues: Lift your hips into a straight line
Push the floor away with your forearm
feel: Work along the side of your trunk, hip and shoulder.
stopIf: Shoulder pain, or back pain increases.
references: McGill SM. Low Back Disorders: Evidence-Based Prevention and Rehabilitation. Human Kinetics.

media.credit: Video: Form for Side Forearm Plank (suzannebowenfitness)

name: Dead bug
why: Teaches your trunk to stay steady while your arms and legs move, the same control you need in every running stride.
setup: Lie on your back with arms pointing at the ceiling and hips and knees bent to 90 degrees.
cues: Lower opposite arm and leg slowly
mistakes: Arching the lower back off the floor

media.credit: Video: Core Exercise: Dead Bug (Children's Hospital Colorado)

name: Glute bridge
why: Strengthens the glutes, which share the load with your lower back and knees when you run, climb stairs and lift.
setup: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat and hip-width apart, arms by your sides.
cues: Squeeze your glutes, then lift your hips
Straight line from knees to shoulders
mistakes: Arching the lower back at the top
Pushing through the toes instead of the heels
Feeling it mostly in the hamstrings (bring your heels a little closer)
feel: Your glutes working. A little in the back of the thighs is fine.
stopIf: Lower-back pain increases during the exercise.

media.credit: Video: Glute Bridge 101 (Knob Noster Physical Therapy)

name: Stair or hill climb

defaultDose.load: Start without a pack; add weight gradually up to your trek load

why: Climbing stairs or hills with a pack is the most specific way to prepare your legs, heart and lungs for trekking. Build the time and pack weight week by week.
setup: Find a long staircase, stair machine or hill.
Wear the boots and pack you'll hike with as you progress.
cues: Walk down slowly to train the knees
feel: Breathing harder, legs working; you can still talk in short sentences.
stopIf: Chest pain, dizziness, or joint pain that changes how you walk.
cautions: Build up slowly if you have knee pain: downhill is the hardest part.

media.credit: Video: Reduce pain hiking uphill and going up stairs by using your glutes (Evolve Flagstaff)
